opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons, and they all kind of stack on top of each other.

The first one is really practical: the world is built for the human form. Our homes, factories, kitchens, hospitals, and tools were all designed around human bodies, with two hands, two legs, and a certain height and reach. If you want a general-purpose robot that can operate anywhere without redesigning the environment around it, the humanoid form factor is the most natural choice. You don't need to rebuild a factory or retrofit a kitchen. The robot just walks in and uses the same stuff we use.

The second reason, which I think is even more important from a research perspective, is data. Data is the lifeblood of these foundation models, and robotics has a huge data problem. You can't scrape robot motor control data from the internet the way you can scrape text for a language model. But a humanoid is closest to us in morphology, which means we can tap into an enormous amount of human data: videos of people doing things, human demonstrations, teleoperation where a person's movements map almost directly onto the robot. The closer the robot's body is to ours, the more of that human experience we can transfer. So the humanoid is not just a hardware bet, it's a data strategy.

And third, there's the generality argument. I believe in building one model and one body that can do many, many tasks, rather than a thousand specialized robots each doing one narrow thing. That's the lesson we learned from language models: a single generalist model ended up beating lots of specialized ones. I think robotics will follow the same path, and the humanoid is the most general body we can bet on.

Finally, the timing feels right. The hardware has gotten much better and cheaper, simulation has improved enormously so we can train in parallel worlds much faster than real time, and foundation models give us reasoning and perception almost for free. When you put those trends together, it feels like humanoid robotics is approaching its own GPT moment. If we get this right, it's not just another research problem. It could be one of the most impactful technologies of our lifetime: physical AI that can actually do useful work in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says homes, factories, kitchens, hospitals, and tools are built around human bodies, making the humanoid form a natural fit.

r002.rationale: It describes humanoids as general-purpose and capable of many tasks, but does not claim they could support any task a reasonable human can perform.

r003.rationale: It notes that hardware has improved and discusses AI, but does not say that developing AI control becomes the central challenge once affordable hardware matures.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the world is built for humans. Every door handle, every staircase, every kitchen counter, every tool in a workshop was designed around the human form factor. So if you want a single robot body that can do the broadest range of useful things without us re-engineering the environment, the humanoid is the most general-purpose shape you can pick. You don't have to rebuild the factory or the home around the robot.

The second reason is data. Robotics has always been bottlenecked on data, not on compute or on algorithms. With humanoids, you get the richest possible transfer from human data. There are billions of hours of video of people doing things with their hands and bodies, and a humanoid is the embodiment that maps most directly onto that. Teleoperation is also far more natural when the robot has your proportions. A person can just put on a headset and move, and the demonstration translates almost one to one.

And third, I think it's the right level of difficulty for a research goal. It's hard enough that you can't cheat your way through it with a narrow trick, so it forces you to solve the real problems: perception, whole-body control, long-horizon planning, learning from simulation and from the web. But it's concrete enough that you know what success looks like. A robot that can walk into an arbitrary home and be useful is a crisp target. That combination of generality and a clear finish line is what makes it compelling to me as a main focus, rather than just one interesting platform among many.

r001.rationale: The response says the world is built for humans and gives human-designed doors, stairs, counters, and tools as examples; a humanoid can work in those spaces without redesigning them.

r002.rationale: It calls the humanoid the most general-purpose shape and says it can handle the broadest range of useful things, but does not claim it could support any task a reasonable human can perform.

r003.rationale: The response discusses data as robotics’ bottleneck and lists AI challenges, but does not say that affordable mature humanoid hardware would make developing the control AI the central challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think humanoids are compelling because we’ve built the world around the human body. Our homes, factories, tools, stairs, doorways—all of those assume a certain shape and a certain way of interacting with the world. If we want a robot that can operate broadly in those environments, a human-like body is a very useful starting point.

There’s also a connection to learning. Humans demonstrate an enormous range of skills, and having a similar body gives a robot a natural correspondence for learning from those demonstrations. That doesn’t make the problem easy, but it gives us a path toward transferring human skills to machines.

What excites me most is the generality. You’re not just building a machine that repeats one motion. You’re asking whether the same embodied intelligence can learn many different tasks and adapt to situations it hasn’t seen before. Humanoids bring that research question into the physical world.

r001.rationale: It says homes, factories, tools, stairs, and doorways were built around the human body, making a human-like body useful in those environments.

r002.rationale: It describes learning many tasks and adapting to new situations, but does not claim a humanoid could support any task a reasonable human can perform.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss affordable, mature humanoid hardware or say that AI control becomes the central challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think humanoid robots are compelling because we’ve built our world around the human body. Our tools, our kitchens, our factories—all of these spaces assume a certain shape and a certain way of interacting. A humanoid has the potential to work in those environments without us having to redesign everything around it.

But what really excites me is the intelligence problem. How do you build one system that can learn many different physical skills, adapt to unfamiliar situations, and turn an instruction into useful action? You can’t solve that by scripting every movement. You need a general-purpose learning system.

The human form also gives us a useful connection to human demonstrations. We have an enormous amount of video showing people doing things. The challenge is turning that visual knowledge into physical competence—understanding how an action works, then actually executing it with balance, contact, and all the uncertainty of the real world.

So, for me, the humanoid is a compelling platform for pursuing general-purpose embodied intelligence. The goal is a robot that can keep learning and become useful across many different tasks.

r001.rationale: It says tools, kitchens, and factories are built around the human body, so humanoids could work there without redesigning those environments.

r002.rationale: It describes a robot becoming useful across many tasks, but does not claim humanoid hardware could support any task a reasonable human can perform.

r003.rationale: It calls general-purpose learning and control an intelligence problem, but does not make the claim conditional on humanoid hardware maturing and becoming affordable.
